title: Structurally different systems are computationally equivalent

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Structurally different systems are computationally equivalent

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because essentially all the kinds of systems studied (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, register machines and others) can emulate each other, a wide variety of systems with very different underlying structures are fundamentally equivalent in the computations they can perform, so computation can be studied abstractly with results applying across systems.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In a sense its most important consequence is that it implies that from a computational point of view a very wide variety of systems, with very different underlying structures, are at some level fundamentally equivalent.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 11, “The Notion of Computation”; section “Implications of Universality” (from p. 674), p. 674. Scope: cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, register machines and other simple programs

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch11-12: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.83

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: For computational expressiveness, classical computability results settle the listed universal systems. The broader prose should not be read as equivalence in efficiency or structure, which the proof does not establish.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define equivalence as equality of computable functions up to effective encoding, then verify mutual simulations or universality for each listed formalism. A formalism unable to realize a computable function realized by another would refute equivalence.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Efficiency and native dynamics are not preserved by universality.

'Fundamentally equivalent' is ambiguous outside computational expressiveness.

fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.8

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: For the families actually constructed in the chapter, mutual emulation is a chain of explicit reductions, and the Church-Turing equivalence says they determine the same class of computations. The constructions are public and finite. The word essentially leaves the boundary of the class slightly soft, but not soft enough to block a check of the systems named.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For the named families, check mutual emulation of a universal member. Confirm if each family can realize exactly the Turing-computable input-output maps; refute if some named family computes a non-Turing function or cannot emulate a Turing machine.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: Equivalence of computable functions does not settle equivalence of runtime, or of behavior from typical initial conditions.

fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.8
data existence: 0.85

data adequacy: 0.75
